Robin's Egg Glazed Vase with Dragon Handles

大清乾隆年製 — Dà Qīng Qiánlóng Nián Zhì · Imperial Flambé-Type Monochrome Glaze, Qianlong Period (1736–1795)

Robin's Egg Glaze (鷓鴣斑釉) Qing Dynasty · Qianlong 1736–1795 Jingdezhen Imperial Kilns Archaistic Form & Dragon Handles Underglaze Impressed Seal Mark Dronova GOM Method

Object Description

The vase belongs to the group of imperial monochrome porcelain of the Qianlong period (1736–1795), produced at the imperial kilns of Jingdezhen. The piece combines an archaistic form with a tall flaring neck and sculptural dragon-form handles with an experimental high-temperature glaze of the Robin's Egg type (鷓鴣斑釉). The surface is covered in a turquoise-blue glaze with characteristic purplish-red mottling and ring-like zones of colour redistribution, formed during reduction firing.

The silhouette — a globular body rising into a tall cylindrical neck with a broadly flaring, trumpet-shaped mouth — reflects the eighteenth-century imperial court's recurring practice of referencing archaic bronze prototypes of the Shang and Zhou periods, a device widely employed in the artistic programme of the Qianlong reign. The proportions and the precision of the profile are consistent with palace-workshop production of the High Qing.

The glaze is the principal diagnostic feature of the piece. Macroscopically it shows a turquoise-blue ground with numerous purplish-red and maroon spots, ring-shaped zones of colour concentration, and smooth transitions between tones, together with pronounced optical depth and a strong vitreous sheen. Each coloured zone shows an individual morphology, without any repeating or mechanically regular pattern — consistent with a natural redistribution of the glaze constituents during high-temperature firing rather than an applied or stencilled effect.

Fig. 4 — Base. Neatly finished footring of dense white porcelain body; the glazed interior of the foot carries the same turquoise-and-maroon mottling. At the centre, a six-character relief seal mark 大清乾隆年製 (Da Qing Qianlong Nian Zhi) is fully covered by the transparent portion of the glaze, with clear character boundaries and regular proportions of the script.

Technological Interpretation

The complex colour pattern of a Robin's Egg glaze arises from the interaction of copper and cobalt oxides within a lead-silicate glassy matrix during reduction firing. Variations in the local degree of reduction and in the local concentration of the colouring oxides give rise to the characteristic purplish-red spotting, turquoise fields, and ring-shaped colour transitions observed on this vessel — a mechanism consistent with an experimental high-temperature glaze of the Qianlong period rather than with any form of applied or painted decoration.

The colour distribution itself is one of the more informative diagnostic criteria for this glaze type: a gradual intensification of the purplish tone in localised areas, natural concentric rings, the absence of sharp colour boundaries, and a soft merging of turquoise and red tones are all consistent with the migration of colouring constituents during melting and the subsequent cooling of the glaze. Complete fusion of the glassy mass, even surface coverage, high transparency of the turquoise ground, and natural — rather than mechanically repeating — irregularity of the colour distribution are further technological indicators of an authentic high-temperature process.

The handles show volumetric, evidently hand-modelled sculpting, with a smooth transition into the body and even glaze coverage, including natural pooling of glaze in the recesses of the coiled forms; no traces of mechanical mould-assembly (e.g. visible seam lines) were identified.

Gemmological Optical Microscopy

Two magnified images of the glaze surface were supplied for this object. Both show a level of resolvable detail — a granular, vitreous matrix, dark speckled inclusions, and a distinct colour-zone boundary — that is broadly consistent with genuine close-up or low-power microscope photography, though the exact instrument and magnification used were not specified and cannot be independently confirmed from the images alone. The descriptions below are limited to what is actually visible.

Zone A — Turquoise Glaze Surface, General Texture

Close-up / Magnification unconfirmed

A pale greenish-white glassy field with a fine, slightly uneven granular texture and scattered small dark (near-black) point inclusions, along with a few faint curved striations within the glaze body. The surface reads as a continuous vitreous layer rather than an applied pigment film. No scale marker is present in the frame, so absolute inclusion size cannot be stated; the described features should be read as qualitative, not measured, observations.

Zone B — Turquoise / Purplish-Red Colour Boundary

Close-up / Magnification unconfirmed

This frame captures the transition between a dense, dark maroon-brown mottled field and an adjoining pale turquoise field. The boundary between the two colour zones is irregular and diffuse rather than a sharp, hard-edged line, with turquoise islands penetrating into the darker field and vice versa — a pattern consistent with the two colour phases having formed together within a single molten glaze during firing, rather than being applied as two separate, later-fused layers. As with Zone A, no scale reference is present, so the observation is qualitative.

Diagnostic Checklist

  • Archaistic globular body with tall, broadly flaring trumpet-shaped mouth
  • Massive, hand-modelled sculptural handles in dragon form
  • Turquoise-blue ground with dense, individually shaped purplish-red and maroon mottling
  • Ring-shaped zones of colour concentration with smooth, non-mechanical transitions
  • High optical depth and pronounced vitreous sheen across the glaze surface
  • Continuous glaze coverage from exterior through the flaring mouth into the throat
  • Even glaze distribution across sculptural handles, no mould-assembly seams
  • Underglaze relief six-character seal mark Da Qing Qianlong Nian Zhi
  • Magnified images show a granular vitreous matrix and a diffuse colour-zone boundary consistent with in-glaze colour migration; exact imaging device/magnification unconfirmed
  • No elemental (XRF/Raman/SEM-EDS) data yet obtained — the conclusion should be treated as preliminary
The combined macroscopic and close-up optical evidence — the archaistic form, the sculptural dragon handles, the non-repeating turquoise-and-purplish-red colour pattern with ring-shaped concentration zones, the continuous glaze coverage into the throat, and the morphology of the underglaze relief mark — is consistent with the technology of experimental high-temperature Robin's Egg (鷓鴣斑釉) monochrome glazes produced at the imperial kilns of Jingdezhen in the second half of the eighteenth century. The two magnified glaze images support, but do not on their own prove, this reading: they show a texture and colour-boundary morphology consistent with an in-glaze (rather than applied) colour effect, but the imaging device and magnification were not confirmed, and no scale reference is present. A conclusive attribution would additionally require elemental analysis (XRF/SEM-EDS) of the glaze and body, and, where possible, Raman spectroscopy of the coloured zones.
